description: How the Roman legion was structured, trained and disciplined into the ancient world's most formidable army.
content_html:
The Backbone of Roman Power

At the heart of Rome’s empire lay an extraordinary military machine. The legion was not simply a fighting force — it was the engine of conquest, colonisation and control. Understanding how the legion was organised tells us a great deal about Roman values: discipline, hierarchy, collective identity, and the expectation that citizens owed military service to the state.

Recruitment and the Citizen-Soldier

In the Imperial period, legionaries were Roman citizens who signed up for a standard term of twenty-five years. Recruits had to be physically fit, of free birth, and free from serious criminal convictions. Provincial men who were not yet citizens could serve in auxiliary units, and on completion of service they were rewarded with Roman citizenship. This arrangement meant the army was also a powerful mechanism for spreading Roman identity across the empire.

Pay was a key incentive. Legionaries received a regular salary, a share of campaign booty, and a substantial land grant or cash payment on discharge. These rewards tied the soldier’s loyalty directly to the general who commanded him — a fact that had enormous political consequences throughout Roman history.

Key Fact

A Roman legion was divided into ten cohorts. Each cohort contained six centuries of around eighty men. Each century was commanded by a centurion — the most important officer in the Roman army’s day-to-day operation.

The Structure of the Legion

The legion’s genius lay in its modular structure. At the top was the legionary legate, a senior senator appointed by the emperor. Below him, six tribunes assisted with administration. The real fighting backbone, however, was the centurion. A centurion was identified by three distinctive features: a transverse crest (crista transversa) on his helmet, a vine stick (vitis) used both as a symbol of authority and an instrument of punishment, and his gladius worn on the left hip — the reverse of ordinary legionaries, who wore theirs on the right. The most senior centurion in a legion, the primus pilus, was a figure of immense prestige.

The first cohort was larger than the rest, containing five double-strength centuries of around 160 men each, giving it a total strength of roughly 800 soldiers. It was the pride of the legion and typically held the position of greatest honour in battle.

At the symbolic heart of every legion stood the aquila — a golden eagle mounted on a staff. The eagle was carried by the aquilifer, one of the most honoured soldiers in the unit. To lose the aquila in battle was one of the greatest disgraces a Roman army could suffer. When three legions under Publius Quinctilius Varus were destroyed in the Teutoburg Forest in 9 AD, the recovery of their lost eagles became a national obsession pursued for decades. The bronze statuette of a legionary held in the British Museum (1867, 0510.4) shows the typical equipment of an Imperial soldier and gives us a vivid material record of how these men looked when on parade.

Training and Discipline

Roman training was systematic and relentless. New recruits practised weapons techniques against a wooden post called a palus, using weapons that were deliberately heavier than standard issue so that the real thing would feel lighter in battle. Soldiers were expected to march twenty Roman miles in five hours in full armour and kit, and to be capable of constructing a fully defended camp at the end of that march.

Discipline was enforced with brutal efficiency. Infractions were punished by flogging; sleeping on duty could mean death. The ultimate collective punishment was decimation, in which one man in ten from a disgraced unit was chosen by lot to be beaten to death by his comrades. Though rarely used, its existence shaped the psychological climate of the legion. This culture of iron discipline had been celebrated in Roman literature for centuries before the Imperial period, and it was seen as a defining national virtue.

Key Fact

Roman legionaries were professional soldiers paid a regular wage. They trained in close-order fighting, engineering and camp-building. The bronze legionary statuette in the British Museum is a key material source for understanding their standard equipment during the Imperial period.

The Greek hoplite phalanx depended on citizen-farmers who owned their own equipment and served for limited seasonal campaigns. The Roman legion, by contrast, was a permanent professional army whose soldiers trained full-time and served for decades. Roman soldiers were also engineers: they could bridge rivers, build siege engines and construct fortified camps, giving the army a strategic flexibility no phalanx could match. Roman legionary coins, such as the Mark Antony Legionary denarius — minted around 32 BC with a galley on one face and an eagle between two standards on the other — were literally struck by generals to pay their troops, showing how tightly military identity and payment were bound together in the Roman system.

The Legionary Fortress

When a legion was stationed in a province, it occupied a permanent legionary fortress. The fortress at Chester (Deva) in Britain is one of the best-preserved examples and is listed as a prescribed material source. A typical fortress was a large rectangular enclosure with a regular internal layout: the headquarters building (principia) at the centre, the commanding officer’s house (praetorium) beside it, barracks blocks for each century arranged in rows, granaries, a hospital and a bathhouse. This regularity — the same layout wherever in the empire a fortress was built — reinforced Roman identity and made it easier for soldiers to function efficiently even in unfamiliar surroundings.
exam_tip_html: When you are asked to ‘describe’ the structure of the Roman army, give specific terminology: legion, cohort, century, centurion, aquila. Avoid vague phrases like “lots of soldiers were organised into groups.” When a source question shows the bronze legionary statuette or the Legionary denarius, use specific details you can see or know about the object — its material, what it shows, where it was found or minted. The examiner’s most common criticism is that students describe sources only in general terms rather than analysing their specific features.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A Roman legion comprised roughly 5,000 citizen-soldiers divided into ten cohorts, each of six centuries commanded by a centurion; the first cohort was the largest and most prestigious.
  • Legionaries were long-service professionals, paid regularly and rewarded with a pension; discipline was severe and the loss of the eagle standard (aquila) was the army’s greatest disgrace.
  • Material sources — including the bronze legionary statuette in the British Museum and the Roman fortress at Chester — give direct evidence for how the legion was equipped and housed.

practice_questions.text: Name the officer who commanded a century in the Roman legion.
Describe the standard structure of a Roman legion.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each accurate point up to three, for example: a legion contained roughly 5,000 to 6,000 soldiers; it was divided into ten cohorts; each cohort was made up of six centuries of around eighty men; each century was commanded by a centurion; the first cohort was double-strength and held the place of greatest honour.

practice_questions.text:
Read this description of a Roman material source: a small bronze statuette, approximately 8 cm tall, showing a soldier standing in a relaxed pose. He wears segmented body armour over a tunic, carries a large rectangular shield, and on his head sits a helmet with cheek-guards. A short sword hangs from his right hip. The figure was found in Britain and is now in the British Museum (1867, 0510.4).

What does this source tell us about the Roman legionary in the Imperial period? Use specific details from the source in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed analysis of specific features of the source (armour, shield, sword, helmet) linked to wider knowledge of the legion's equipment and organisation. The response considers what the source confirms and what it cannot tell us (e.g. it shows parade or off-duty dress, not necessarily battle formation). At least two specific details are used analytically.
Secure: Clear use of specific details from the source, linked to accurate knowledge of the legionary's role. Some consideration of what the source reveals or limits.
Developing: General reference to the source with limited specific detail; knowledge of the legion mainly descriptive.
Emerging: Minimal engagement with the source; knowledge vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why training and discipline were important to the success of the Roman legion.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each accurate point plus 1 mark for development, up to four marks. Points might include: rigorous weapons training meant soldiers could fight effectively in close order; heavy training weapons meant real equipment felt lighter in battle; the ability to march twenty miles and then build a camp gave the army strategic flexibility; severe punishments (flogging, decimation) maintained collective discipline and prevented cowardice; standardised training meant soldiers from different parts of the empire could fight together effectively.

practice_questions.text: How useful is the Roman fortress at Chester as evidence for understanding the Roman army in the Imperial period?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced analysis weighing the site's specific strengths (regular layout revealing hierarchy and function, barracks showing how centuries were housed, presence of hospital and bathhouse indicating permanent settlement) against limitations (the site has been altered over time; we cannot know the day-to-day experience of soldiers from the architecture alone). Named features of the site are used precisely.
Secure: Clear discussion of what the fortress reveals, with some acknowledgement of limitations. Specific features are named.
Developing: Mainly descriptive account of the fortress with limited evaluative comment.
Emerging: Vague reference to the fortress; limited accurate knowledge.

practice_questions.text: How important was discipline to the Roman army? Use a range of evidence in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained argument that evaluates discipline as central to Roman military effectiveness, supported by specific evidence (training with the palus, punishment by flogging, decimation as collective terror, the aquila as a symbol demanding collective commitment). The response also considers discipline alongside other factors (professional pay and rewards, engineeering skills, modular organisation) and reaches a supported judgement on the relative importance of discipline. Named sources are integrated.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant evidence and sustained explanation. Some range of points; a supported conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant points about discipline but limited range; explanation may be underdeveloped or one-sided.
Emerging: Simple points; evidence limited or missing; may retell facts without argument.

What was the aquila in the Roman army?
options: The golden eagle standard of the legion

knowledge_checks.q: Each century in the Roman legion was commanded by an officer called a _____.
Non-citizen soldiers who served alongside Roman legions were known as _____ troops.
Match each term to its correct meaning:
right: The most senior centurion in a legion
The collective punishment of killing one in ten soldiers
The golden eagle standard carried into battle

flashcard_questions.a: The main unit of the Roman army, comprising roughly 5,000 to 6,000 citizen soldiers.

flashcard_questions.q: How many cohorts formed a standard Roman legion?
What officer commanded a century in the Roman legion?
What was the aquila, and why did its loss matter?
flashcard_questions.a: The legion's golden eagle standard; losing it in battle was a catastrophic national disgrace.
The most senior centurion in a legion, commanding the first century of the first cohort.

flashcard_questions.q: How could a non-citizen earn Roman citizenship through military service?
flashcard_questions.a: By serving in an auxiliary unit and completing the full term of service.

flashcard_questions.q: What was decimation as a military punishment?
flashcard_questions.a: One man in ten from a disgraced unit was selected by lot and beaten to death by his comrades.

flashcard_questions.q: What training tool did Roman recruits use to practise sword-fighting?
flashcard_questions.a: The palus — a heavy wooden post used as a striking target.

flashcard_questions.q: The Roman fortress at Chester is a prescribed material source. What does it reveal about the legion?
flashcard_questions.a: Its regular internal layout shows how centuries were housed and the hierarchy of the legion.

flashcard_questions.q: Which material source in the British Museum shows the equipment of an Imperial Roman soldier?
What symbol appeared on the reverse of the Mark Antony Legionary denarius?
flashcard_questions.a: An eagle between two military standards.

glossary_terms.definition: The main unit of the Roman army, consisting of roughly 5,000 to 6,000 citizen soldiers divided into cohorts and centuries.
Non-citizen units attached to the Roman army, often recruited from allied peoples and providing specialist skills such as archery or cavalry.
The commanding officer of a Roman legion, typically a senator appointed by the emperor.
An officer commanding a century of roughly eighty men, identified by a transverse helmet crest (crista transversa), a vine stick (vitis) of authority, and a gladius worn on the left hip.
The golden eagle standard of a Roman legion, carried into battle by the aquilifer; its loss was a catastrophic disgrace.
A wooden stake used as a training target by Roman recruits learning to thrust and cut with sword and shield.
